                         THE HARBOURMASTER'S LEDGER OF HYSHEILROADS
                      Volume Two -- The One Hundred and Twenty Berths
============================================================================================

This book is the standing record of the one hundred and twenty berths of Hysheilroads, kept
by the harbourmaster and copied fair at the close of each quarter. It is set down in the
form the outer office requires, which is to say: a roster of what is on the roll, followed
by the entries taken on the rounds, followed by whatever notes the clerks thought worth
keeping.

The berths are numbered from 1 to 120 and always in the same direction, berth 1 being the
westernmost on the reach and berth 120 the easternmost. West means a lower berth number and
east a higher one, and an entry that speaks of walking or sailing east is speaking of
counting upward. Nothing in this book uses any other convention.

Ten things are recorded against every berth, and there are exactly one hundred and twenty of
each on the roll. Every berth has one keeper and no berth shares a keeper with another. The
same holds of the creature kept at the berth, of the cargo standing against it, of the home
port declared for it, of the pennant flown from it, of the ailment entered against it in the
quarter's health return, of the watch shift it is worked under, of the rig carried by the
craft that lies there, of the beacon shown from its head, and of the toll band under which
its dues are reckoned. The roster in Part One lists all ten rolls in full; it does not say
which berth any of them belongs to, and that is the whole of what this book is for.

The numbered entries in Part Two are the round record. Every one of them is true as written.
They were taken by different clerks on different days and in no particular order, and a
great many of them say the same thing twice over in different words, which is the ordinary
condition of a ledger and not an error in it. Between the entries the clerks have set down
the state of the tide, the weather, the condition of the quay, the stores drawn, the dues
taken and whatever else was passing; none of that bears on the berths and none of it should
be read as though it did.

What the office claims for the numbered entries is exactly this: that every one of them is
true of the standing table as it stood at the close of the quarter, and that taken together
they settle that table one way and no other. The office does not claim that they are the
fewest entries which would settle it, and they are certainly not. This book is a record of
rounds walked, and a great deal of it says twice or three times over what has already been
said once.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

is the order the clerk happened to write them in and carries no meaning whatever.

PART TWO -- THE INSPECTION RECORD
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------


SECTION 1 -- The western berths, first round

The office clock was found a quarter of a chain out of upright and was packed level. The
deputy of the reach went over the entries for the Slaneirnyard rig and let them stand. Work
on the eastern approach was stopped by a squall that took one glass to pass over and taken
up again after. The office received a circular about the form of headings and filed it
unread. The quay walls were pointed along one stretch and the work was passed by the clerk
on loan from the outer office.

    1.  Carried over from the page before, where the ink had run: The Nivuithric keeper lies
        at an odd-numbered berth. Confirmed at the evening tally and carried forward
        unchanged.
    2.  The inner basin round gave this and the outer round did not contradict it: The
        Thiakwyn keeper and the Selleurn creature occupy adjacent berths. Nobody has found
        cause to go behind this entry.
    3.  Written while the matter was fresh and not improved upon afterwards: The Plilirurn
        creature is berthed immediately east of the Lournainarne pennant, with nothing
        between them. It agrees with the survey papers, which were consulted afterwards. The
        matter was plain and the entry is plain with it.
    4.  The rough book, the slate and the fair copy all agree here: The Ruigriarythe home
        port and the Choaflame beacon are not recorded at the same berth. It was confirmed
        on the round following and carried forward. This was checked from the water as well
        as from the quay.

The fair copy was left open overnight and the ink smudged along one edge. A survey of the
wall behind berth 56 was ordered in the spring and is outstanding. The Mudrilyard rig stands
in the quarter's summary exactly as it stands here. The account for the Flaendouturn watch
remains open pending a weight certificate. The Snektithe toll band is one of the entries the
copyist marked for attention and then let alone.

    5.  Established on the round and not afterwards disputed: The Pergale watch precedes the

SECTION 7 -- The quarter's carried-forward entries

The Nailfever ailment has been on the roll for as long as anybody in the office remembers.

A heavy dew wet the whole quay before dawn and was gone by the middle of the forenoon. The
tide was late by the best part of a glass and the office clock was blamed for it. The tide
stood turning while the round was walked for longer than the table allows, and the reason is
not known. The wind stood in one quarter for six days together and then went right round in
a night. Frost lay on the coping until the opening of the gates and made the walking slow.

The warden of the outer moorings entered a dry wind from the shoals against the forenoon and

Paint for the coming quarter was ordered early on account of the opening of the year. The

with the flood and dropped with the ebb, as it does here in the wet months. The Tralliadmash

SECTION 8 -- Observations at the change of the watch

The weather in the opening of the year was as it usually is, and the book records nothing
further about it. A wind off the water carried spray the length of the quay and wet the
entries as they were made. Weather held fair for the whole of the round and the entries were
made in comfort. The copyist reports sleet on and off all afternoon and adds that the round
was walked anyway. There was a warm damp that got into the paper at the start of the round
and something very like it at the end.

  756.  Agreed at the muster with nobody dissenting: There are exactly 11 berths separating
        the Hirmioling creature from the Friathaegale watch. Read back to the keeper, who
        assented without qualification.
  757.  One of the findings the outer office asked to have set out plainly: The Vreiledresin
        cargo falls in the eastern stretch, berths 95 through 120. Nobody has found cause to
        go behind this entry.
  758.  The inner basin round gave this and the outer round did not contradict it: The
        Plaermasprit rig lies somewhere to the west of the Niothreth home port.

The demurrage account was settled and the papers filed with the quarter's. Payment was
refused on one account and the matter passed to the outer office. Dues for the week came to
less than the week before, the reach being quieter. The tally clerk asks that dues be taken
at the gate rather than on the quay. The cash box was counted at the last glass of the
middle watch and agreed with the day's entries.

  759.  Copied from the slate before the rain took it off: The Jearrenlull watch is berthed
        somewhere west of the Giveiclew rig, though not necessarily beside it. The rough
        book agrees, and so does the copy held in the outer office. The finding was not
        contested by anybody present.
  760.  Reading west to east, the Praestomebb watch comes before the Hostariff toll band,
        and the Hostariff toll band before the Saeteistithe toll band. This one the outer
        office copied without comment. This line was not disputed by anybody with standing
        to dispute it.

A perished rope was reported by a keeper and found to have been repaired already. Weather
for the week: wind and no rain, which is unusual here on four days and nothing remarkable on
the others. The quarter is entered as ordinary, which in this office is the highest praise
available. A split fender was found at berth 101 and made safe before the round moved on.
The wind backed twice before the turn of the glass and settled very near where it had begun.

  761.  Entered after the round was walked a second time on the same day: The Ryrnosvek
        keeper lies somewhere to the west of the Dodoasyard rig.
  762.  The pilot had this from the quay and the quay had it from the round: None of the
        following lie in berths 12 through 31: the Briolyrn creature, the Gougarnaemia
        ailment and the Gliquota toll band. The ink is clear here and the reading is not in
        doubt.

The apron at berth 55 drains the wrong way and puddles after hard frost that held until the
middle of the day. A hand lamp was found burning at berth 70 in daylight and was put out. A
loose plank at berth 27 was nailed down and the nail heads punched below the surface. The
hard standing at berth 17 is breaking up at the edges and wants attention. The mooring rings
at berth 19 were counted and all were present.

  763.  Entered in the rough book that forenoon and copied here without change: None of the

        letter for letter.
  764.  The Vekoalwick beacon occupies an even-numbered berth. The clerk initialled it and

  766.  On the authority of the keeper of the book, who was present throughout: The

        copies.
  767.  The rough book has it in these words, and so does this: The Quatesosis ailment
        precedes the Slatroamarne pennant, which in turn precedes the Chartaerorne home
        port, reading west to east. Filed with the quarter's papers and not needed since.

The reach was calm enough at dawn to see the bottom at the steps, which is remarked on
rarely. A fog came up the reach with the flood and went out again with the ebb. There was
hard frost that held until the middle of the day from first light, and the round was walked
in it without complaint. The glass fell a full division between the quarter bell and dusk,
which is usually a hard night. Snow lay on the quay for the better part of two days and was
swept into the water.

  768.  Entered without query and initialled by the clerk on duty: The Measkeryrn creature

A heavy dew wet the whole quay before dawn and was gone by the middle of the forenoon. The
tide was barely moving and the wind against it, which is the condition that makes the
narrows awkward. The wind rose with the flood and dropped with the ebb, as it does here in
the autumn. There was a dry wind from the shoals, and the lamps were lit two hours earlier
than the season wants. There was thunder offshore during the middle watch and none of it
came ashore.

The weighbridge was out of true by a hand's breadth and was not corrected until later. The
Nokranrate toll band was among the entries read aloud when the book was closed. Berth 85 was
inspected at the second bell after noon and nothing was entered against it. The night clerk
reports the stores in good order and the dues fully collected. The apron at berth 10 drains
the wrong way and puddles after hard frost that held until the middle of the day.

 1228.  The Triallourn creature and the Kloadette pennant are not recorded at the same

 1229.  Given to the clerk by the quay warden directly and taken as good: Between the

The deputy of the reach notes the Droafainvang rig as satisfactory and moves on without
elaborating. The chain at berth 84 was shortened by two links at the keeper's request. The
glass fell all day and nothing came of it, which is entered for the record. The warden of
the outer moorings reports the whole reach in fair order excepting the matters entered
above. Weather for the week: low cloud and no wind at all on four days and nothing
remarkable on the others.

        correction.

A queue formed at the water point and the officer of stores set an order of use for the rest
of the week. The water in the basin was fouled by an overturned load and cleared by the
following day. A cutter was refused entry for want of papers and was admitted the following
day. A blocked gully was found during the round and made safe until the masons can come. A
hoy broke down in the entrance and was warped clear by hand.

The Brairryweed cargo is one of the entries the copyist marked for attention and then let

The first entry for the Muizekurn creature in this book was struck and written again below.
The Vremresin cargo was mentioned in the quarter's return and in no other paper.

Dues outstanding at the close of the quarter came to nothing at all, which is rare. The

The tide ran turning while the round was walked and carried a quantity of weed onto the

Berth 20 is the only one on its stretch with a working standpipe. The deputy of the reach

Oakum was drawn from the store and signed for by the deputy of the reach. Dues were remitted

The reach stood empty for the better part of a day, which the office cannot account for. The
coping is out of true by a quarter of a chain along the middle of the quay and has been
entered as such. The inner basin was crowded enough that a flat-bottomed boat was turned
away and came back on the next tide. A pilot boat went aground on the bank and floated off
without help on the next flood. The gates were opened at the turn of the tide and the first
craft through was a lighter.

The weighbridge was tested against the standard and found true within the tolerance allowed.

The reach carried more traffic in the opening of the year than in any quarter the book

SECTION 13 -- The chandler's week

The office received a circular about the form of headings and filed it unread. Growth was
scraped from the steps at berth 6, which were dangerous before. The warden of the inner
basin reports the crane at the head of the quay sound, having had it tested. The clerk asked
whether the Zoachumeal cargo should be entered at all and was told that it should. The guard
rail at berth 66 stands the length of a boat hook short of the height the orders set.

 1286.  Carried into this book from the survey papers without alteration: Not one of the

 1287.  The Girtokrot ailment precedes the Bryktallow cargo, which in turn precedes the

 1289.  The officer of the reach saw it himself and required no corroboration: The
        Krurdylevy toll band and the Haembelboom rig are not recorded at the same berth.
        This one the outer office copied without comment. That much is certain and is
        entered as certain.

The assistant tallyman signed the quarter's return and sent it upriver by the usual hand.
The quarter is the third in succession in which no berth has been taken out of service. The
master of the weighbridge remarks that the quarter passed without a single serious dispute.
A complete reading of the roll was made at the close and no discrepancy was found. The
quarter is entered as ordinary, which in this office is the highest praise available.

 1290.  Copied into the fair book the same evening and not altered since: One and the same
        berth carries the Zassounlevy toll band and the Jiartyturn watch. Nobody has found
        cause to go behind this entry.
 1291.  Set down here because the standing orders require it to be set down: Sailing east,
        the three are met in this order: the Mirkoulbeam beacon, then the Gougarnaemia
        ailment, then the Gertispar rig. The matter was plain and the entry is plain with
        it. The rough book has it identically, down to the wording.

Nothing was entered under weather for three days together, the sky having done nothing worth
the ink. The weather in the spring was as it usually is, and the book records nothing
further about it. Hail at the last glass of the middle watch drove everybody indoors and
stopped the tally for a quarter of an hour. The weather glass was tapped, read, and the
reading entered without comment. A heavy dew wet the whole quay before dawn and was gone by
the middle of the forenoon.

 1292.  Entered without query and initialled by the clerk on duty: Sailing east, the three
        are met in this order: the Liagremwake watch, then the Droaduidvas keeper, then the
        Glankovigil watch. Nothing in the later rounds contradicted it.
 1293.  Given to the clerk by the quay warden directly and taken as good: The Plaimsalt
        cargo lies somewhere to the west of the Stenmark toll band. No hand has been laid on
        this line since it was written. The line was gone over in ink after the pencil
        faded, and not otherwise changed.
 1294.  Sailing east, the three are met in this order: the Gostymeal cargo, then the
        Brakroulric keeper, then the Nokranrate toll band. The slate agreed before it was
        wiped, for what that is worth. It has been true in every book the office holds.
 1295.  The berth number of the Kiathisrate toll band is greater than the berth number of
        the Prolband toll band. Read back to the keeper, who assented without qualification.
        The entry was made, read, and left as made.

The tide was late by the best part of a glass and the office clock was blamed for it. The
tally clerk reports fog standing in the roads and adds that the round was walked anyway.
There was a wind that got up at dusk and dropped before dawn at the start of the round and
something very like it at the end. The wind rose with the flood and dropped with the ebb, as
it does here in the autumn. Frost lay on the coping until the second glass of the forenoon
and made the walking slow.

 1296.  Neither queried nor amended since the day it was taken: The Horraband toll band is
        berthed somewhere west of the Trafairalt home port, though not necessarily beside

 1297.  A finding of the survey, carried across into the round record: Exactly 12 berths lie

 1298.  The pilot had this from the quay and the quay had it from the round: The Drescale

The summary was written at the close and the detail behind it stands in the entries above.
The copyist notes that the standing orders were read aloud twice in the quarter, as

The wind stood in one quarter for six days together and then went right round in a night.
The copyist entered a dry cold with the air very clear against the forenoon and nothing at
all against the afternoon. The tide came in setting hard to the east and went out the same
way, which is worth entering only because it is rare. Nothing was entered under weather for
three days together, the sky having done nothing worth the ink. The reach lay under a wind
that got up at dusk and dropped before dawn until the tide turned, and cleared within the
hour.

 1402.  Nobody has queried this since it was entered, and nobody is likely to: The Fovestock

The deputy of the reach asks that the weather be entered before the tide and not after, as
the form requires. The glass moved not at all for three days, which the copyist says is the
worst sign of the lot. The morning clerk entered the weather twice and the tide not at all,
which has been corrected in the fair copy. The clerk who keeps the rough book holds that the
tide table is a glass out and has said so in each of the turn of the year books. The reach
was calm enough at dawn to see the bottom at the steps, which is remarked on rarely.


SECTION 14 -- Entries taken in poor light

Stores were drawn against the quarter's allowance and the balance noted below. A visiting
clerk copied three pages of this book and took the copies away with him. Nothing came up the
reach between the second glass of the forenoon and dawn, which the night clerk entered with
some relief. Nothing was landed on the north quay that morning; the cranes stood idle until
the first bell. The master of the weighbridge was called away and the round was finished by
the officer who walks the eastern end.

The quay was clear of stacked goods by the reading of the standing orders, which the
standing orders require and which rarely happens. The reach carried more traffic in the
opening of the year than in any quarter the book records. Work on the eastern approach was
stopped by smoke from the tar sheds and taken up again after. The steps at the western end
are worn the length of a boat hook below the line they were cut to. The weighbridge was
tested against the standard and found true within the tolerance allowed.

The quarter is the third in succession in which no berth has been taken out of service. The
quarter's weather was as bad as the wet months and rather better than the one before. One
page of the quarter's book was spoiled and recopied, and both copies are held. The quarter
is entered as ordinary, which in this office is the highest praise available. The rounds
were walked on every day the orders require and on four days besides.

The bar shoaled through the quiet season and has since scoured out again on its own. The

The tally was read back aloud and agreed, which is not always the case. Snow lay on the quay

The quarter ended with the whole reach in service and no berth out of use. The quarter is

A heavy dew wet the whole quay before dawn and was gone by the middle of the forenoon. The

wind in the wet months took the frost off the quay in a single forenoon.

 1503.  The under-harbourmaster is satisfied, having walked the ground himself: Of the

The Durholm home port is entered above the line and should have been entered below it. Berth

cannot account for.


SECTION 15 -- The inner basin

The warden of the outer moorings keeps the rough book in pencil and is not to be talked out

        these words through two fair copies.
 1549.  Written into the margin first and moved here when the fair copy was made: Not one of
        the following is berthed between 4 and 20 inclusive: the Slamvas keeper, the
        Putreamusk creature, the Triallourn creature, the Tiabukern home port and the
        Lessuislevy toll band.

A note against the Frorriokmash cargo asks for a further inspection and does not say why.
The tide stood setting west against the wind for longer than the table allows, and the
reason is not known. The second clerk notes the Blealorne home port as satisfactory and
moves on without elaborating. The clerk of the outer berths notes that hard frost that held
until the middle of the day is entered against the wrong day in the rough book. A survey of
the wall behind berth 96 was ordered in the autumn and is outstanding.

 1550.  Written up from the slate before it was wiped for the next round: The Spoaraemast
        rig and the Skoarnern home port are recorded at the same berth. Filed with the
        quarter's papers and not needed since.
 1551.  The inspector of holds reports, and the harbourmaster has countersigned: The
        Preistuisoc keeper occupies an even-numbered berth. Struck once in error and written
        again identically beneath.
 1552.  The Bopernalt home port and the Groalyrgaff rig are recorded at the same berth. It
        is entered in the summary in these same terms.
 1553.  Established on the round and not afterwards disputed: The berth number of the
        Stusrate toll band is greater than the berth number of the Zadigale watch. The
        finding was not contested by anybody present. This line was not disputed by anybody
        with standing to dispute it.

A shallop was held at the entrance until the outgoing traffic had cleared. Silt was carted
from the head of the basin and tipped where the orders require. Two of the four capstans
were out of service for the week and the work went round them. A queue formed at the water
point and the keeper of the lamp store set an order of use for the rest of the week. A loose
coping stone was reported by a keeper and found to have been repaired already.

 1554.  The rough book has it in these words, and so does this: The Ploudvas keeper precedes
        the Meizuidmeal cargo, which in turn precedes the Rosalard creature, reading west to
        east. The clerk read it back and the keeper let it pass.
 1555.  The stretch from berth 69 to berth 73 holds none of the following: the Skesonbark
        cargo, the Demboadreth home port, the Lousuillosis ailment, the Klorkothosis
        ailment, the Jearrombeam beacon and the Shirmothrate toll band. The rough book
        agrees, and so does the copy held in the outer office. The entry stands as the round
        left it.
 1556.  From the day's findings, in the order they were taken: The berth number of the
        Skesonbark cargo is greater than the berth number of the Gulwilt ailment. Read back
        to the keeper, who assented without qualification. Confirmed at the evening tally
        and carried forward unchanged.
 1557.  Carried over from the page before, where the ink had run: Walking the quay eastward,
        the inspector reaches the Tiabukern home port before the Notigrist cargo. Entered
        last in the run and checked first on the round after.

The roll was read through at the close of the quarter and every entry on it accounted for.
The ladder at berth 18 was reported unsound and roped off for the week. The lamp standard at
berth 84 was relit at the forenoon muster. The drain cover at berth 106 was lifted and
replaced the wrong way round. The glass fell all day and nothing came of it, which is
entered for the record.

 1558.  Set down at the water point while the tally was going on: The Slaneirnyard rig lies
        immediately to the west of the Brirriarnusk creature. No hand has been laid on this
        line since it was written.
 1559.  Entered against the round of that forenoon: The Stathan keeper lies within the first
        16 berths of the reach. The entry was made, read, and left as made. The keeper was
        shown the entry and made no remark.

Payment was refused on one account and the matter passed to the outer office. The office
lamp was refilled twice in the week, which is more than usual. The copy sent upriver differs
from this one only in the spelling of the headings. A visiting officer asked after the
Woaskonmor keeper and was shown the relevant page. The office's tide table was replaced and
the old one kept for comparison.

 1560.  Read at the gate, entered at the office, and not since disturbed: The berth 10 entry
        rules out the Spipovang rig. This was among the lines read aloud when the book was

 1561.  Set down here because the standing orders require it to be set down: The
        Braebeispark beacon lies somewhere to the east of the Plaikeanband toll band. The
        line was numbered, initialled and left alone. Nothing further was added to this line
        in the whole of the quarter.
 1562.  Written out again after the first entry was spoiled: The Trafothorne home port lies
        somewhere to the west of the Vreiledresin cargo. It agrees with the survey papers,
        which were consulted afterwards.
 1563.  From the rough book, in the words the clerk used at the time: The Kriodrournax
        creature lies somewhere to the east of the Snaelel creature. Both rounds of that day

 1564.  Held back one day for confirmation and then entered as it stood: The Ronkumquota
        toll band stands in the very next berth west of the Spomoudquota toll band. It was

Nothing has been entered against the Zadigale watch since the book was opened. Lamp oil was
drawn from the store and signed for by the night clerk. The file relating to the Lakairlamp
beacon was sent for and came back the following day. Rain got into the ledger chest and
three pages had to be dried and rebound. A complaint about noise from the tar sheds was
received and passed on unaltered.

 1565.  Held over from the morning and entered when the light improved: The Peishemgaff rig
        and the Plirnysume pennant are recorded at the same berth. This one the office has
        never had cause to query.
 1566.  The under-harbourmaster is satisfied, having walked the ground himself: The Drodtide
        watch is berthed somewhere west of the Veigousmash cargo, though not necessarily
        beside it. Agreed by both clerks present and initialled by the senior of them. Both
        the rough book and the slate had it this way before the slate was wiped.
 1567.  Entered from the pilot's own account of the reach: The Joundilboom rig and the
        Gyrbeam beacon lie side by side. Taken as settled from that day, and nothing since
        has unsettled it. The entry was witnessed and is held to be good.
 1568.  Recorded by the officer of the reach, who had it from the keeper: Sailing east, the
        three are met in this order: the Vripoamund home port, then the Jabring creature,
        then the Birlelmash cargo. It has been true in every book the office holds. The ink
        is clear here and the reading is not in doubt.

A pilot boat was refused entry for want of papers and was admitted the following day. The
night clerk finds the drainage along the whole quay worse than in the spring and says so
plainly. The bar shoaled through the short days and has since scoured out again on its own.
The reach stood empty for the better part of a day, which the office cannot account for. The
clerk on loan from the outer office reports the whole reach in fair order excepting the
matters entered above.

 1569.  The Shistiakell keeper lies immediately to the west of the Nokranrate toll band.
        Struck once in error and written again identically beneath.
 1570.  Taken as good on the authority of the clerk who walked the stretch: One and the same
        berth carries the Mapaeswick beacon and the Hirmioling creature. The matter was
        plain and the entry is plain with it.
 1571.  Of the matters settled that week, this was the least contested: Exactly 1 berth lie
        between the Bloamiflame beacon and the Pozaenkell keeper. It was written in good
        light and there is no doubt about the reading. No amendment has been entered against
        it since.
 1572.  Fixed beyond argument at the evening tally: The Baemostallow cargo is berthed
        immediately beside the Mirkoulbeam beacon. The clerk of the outer berths saw it and
        had nothing to add. This one the outer office copied without comment.

Work on the eastern approach was stopped by a warm damp that got into the paper and taken up
again after. The ledger chest was moved to the dry side of the office after the rain got in.
The Vreiledresin cargo was not inspected this quarter, the last inspection being recent
enough. The Kasting creature was recorded in the round hand the outer office insists on and
is difficult to make out. Hail at the last glass of the middle watch drove everybody indoors
and stopped the tally for a quarter of an hour.

 1573.  This was the finding of the round and is entered as such: The Drutyndar keeper is
        berthed no further west than berth 110. Filed with the quarter's papers and not
        needed since.
 1574.  Nobody has queried this since it was entered, and nobody is likely to: The
        Jearrenlull watch falls in the western stretch, berths 1 through 4. The rough book
        agrees, and so does the copy held in the outer office. This line was copied twice
        and reads the same both times.
 1575.  Entered after the round was walked a second time on the same day: The Tortosorne
        home port is berthed immediately east of the Sputholgaff rig, with nothing between
        them. Nothing was added to it and nothing taken away.
 1576.  A plain finding, and entered in the plain form: The Spusdar keeper is berthed
        somewhere east of the Vrithalvask home port, though not necessarily beside it. The

 1577.  One of the quarter's plain findings, entered here in order: The Depiscar home port

The under-harbourmaster asked that the Veakriflake cargo be looked at again in the next

Nothing further was entered until the following forenoon. A boy was sent for a fresh quire
of paper and did not come back before the change of the watch. The book was closed at the
setting of the night watch and opened again the following forenoon.

 1578.  A finding of the survey, carried across into the round record: The Frikreamash cargo
        is not berthed at berth 87. The clerk initialled it and the harbourmaster let it
        stand. This was checked a second time on the following round and found good.
 1579.  The Saeteistithe toll band and the Zaingodvask home port are recorded at the same

The allowance for sailcloth was raised and the increase noted for the outer office. Dues
were taken at the forenoon muster and the receipts entered against the quarter. The store
was locked and the key held by the assistant tallyman for the whole of the week. Hand lamps
for the coming quarter was ordered early on account of the turn of the year. A dispute about
the rate of dues was settled by reference to the standing orders.

 1580.  Entered in the rough book that forenoon and copied here without change: The stretch

 1581.  Noted at the change of the watch by both the outgoing and the incoming clerk: The

The morning clerk queried a payment and it was found to have been entered twice. The store
of ink and paper ran out before the end of the week and more was sent for. Buckets was
ordered, delivered short, and the shortfall entered. The quarter's dues were carried to the
outer office by hand and receipted there. The demurrage account was settled and the papers
filed with the quarter's.

 1582.  Set down while the round was still walking and left as written: The berth number of

 1583.  The Snokialwilt ailment lies somewhere to the west of the Jaisimark toll band. This

The surveyor of the quay remarks that the Dioskuturn watch was the subject of a query in the
previous book. The summary was written at the close and the detail behind it stands in the
entries above. The Vrarlionwick beacon is carried forward from the previous book without
change. Dues were collected at the first glass of the afternoon and the receipts entered in
the other book. The book for the quarter runs to more pages than the last, the reach being
busier.

 1584.  Written into the margin first and moved here when the fair copy was made: One and

A visiting clerk from upriver spent two days in the office and took away three copies. A
list of the office's books was made and is kept inside the lid of the chest. The office
window was broken in a raw easterly that emptied the quay and boarded until the glazier
came. The copyist was set to work on the previous book and made slow progress. The deputy of
the reach asks that the outer office send the forms earlier in the spring.

 1586.  Confirmed by two clerks working independently of one another: The Haivothing

 1587.  From the tally clerk's own book, copied word for word: There are exactly 1 berth
        separating the Stiofuisusk creature from the Snukairnel creature. It was the

        round after.
 1588.  Entered in ink at once, the matter being plain enough: The Friozaelorne home port
        lies within the first 29 berths of the reach. That much is certain and is entered as
        certain. It has stood in these words through two fair copies.

The Swabiolmeal cargo appears in the outer office copy under a slightly different heading.
There was a swell that never broke for most of the day, which slowed the round but did not
stop it. The clerk who keeps the rough book reports a mist that never lifted above the
coping and adds that the round was walked anyway. The Brubrerdar keeper has been on the roll
for as long as anybody in the office remembers. Dues for the quarter came in short and the
difference is accounted for elsewhere.

 1589.  Reading west to east, the Skeshaeflare beacon comes before the Quombaelling
        creature, and the Quombaelling creature before the Theshawick beacon. This line was

 1590.  Given to the clerk by the quay warden directly and taken as good: The berth number

        before the light went and needs no correction.
 1591.  The harbourmaster asked for this in writing and here it is: The Briolyrn creature
        does not share a berth with the Prakish pennant. No hand has been laid on this line

 1592.  One of the findings the outer office asked to have set out plainly: The Kloulboom
        rig is berthed somewhere east of the Putreamusk creature, though not necessarily

 1593.  Set down at the water point while the tally was going on: The Ziomaegaff rig is

A second clerk went over the figures for the Vaerkoulwake watch and found them right. The

 1596.  Put down in the plain form the outer office asks for: One and the same berth carries

The Tholouvang rig was entered by the night clerk and initialled by the morning one. The

 1598.  This was settled early in the round and nothing later unsettled it: The Girtokrot

 1599.  The under-harbourmaster is satisfied, having walked the ground himself: The

The clerk of the outer berths walked berth 114 twice, the second time in better light. The
papers relating to the Laifiontorch beacon are held in the outer office and were not

the close of the wet months. The Begrekume pennant is written in ink over a pencil line that
has not been rubbed out. The reach was calm enough at dawn to see the bottom at the steps,
which is remarked on rarely.

 1600.  Checked on the ground and checked again in the book: The Dyllianreth home port is
        berthed somewhere east of the Jiartyturn watch, though not necessarily beside it.
        The entry was made, read, and left as made.
 1601.  Attested by two hands at the change of the watch: Walking the quay eastward, the
        inspector reaches the Zassounlevy toll band before the Sakrinythe home port. The
        entry was witnessed by a clerk who had no part in making it.

The weather glass was tapped, read, and the reading entered without comment. The tide stood
running hard through the narrows for longer than the table allows, and the reason is not
known. The wind stood in one quarter for six days together and then went right round in a
night. Hail at the middle watch drove everybody indoors and stopped the tally for a quarter
of an hour. The weather in the spring was as it usually is, and the book records nothing
further about it.

 1602.  Entered against the round of that forenoon: The Chachasoc keeper is berthed
        somewhere west of the Jykroresin cargo, though not necessarily beside it. The clerk
        of the outer berths saw it and had nothing to add.
 1603.  Entered without query and initialled by the clerk on duty: The Gortireth home port
        is berthed no further east than berth 29. Nothing in the quarter has told against
        it. The keeper was shown the entry and made no remark.

Dues outstanding at the close of the quarter came to nothing at all, which is rare. The
summary above was agreed between the clerks before it was copied fair. Nothing entered in
this quarter contradicts anything entered in the last. Three matters stood over at the close
of the quarter and all three are entered elsewhere. The quarter ended with the whole reach
in service and no berth out of use.

 1604.  Taken as good on the authority of the clerk who walked the stretch: The Briagreorne
        home port lies within the last 12 berths of the reach. It is entered in the summary

 1605.  Entered under the standing orders and needing no further authority: The Flisiolaemia
        ailment is berthed somewhere west of the Vaeshyktorch beacon, though not necessarily

 1606.  The Ryrnosvek keeper stands in the very next berth west of the Snudurglass watch.
        The entry was made before the light went and needs no correction.

Berth 94 and the two beside it were inspected in one pass to save walking. The inkwells were

outer office copy, which is an omission there. The warden of the inner basin found the gate
at berth 62 unlocked and locked it himself.

 1607.  Held back one day for confirmation and then entered as it stood: The Larrydar keeper
        and the Skorriordue toll band are not recorded at the same berth. The slate agreed

 1608.  One of the quarter's plain findings, entered here in order: None of the following

The copyist notes the Gaisenstay rig as satisfactory and moves on without elaborating. The

The file relating to the Durloasitis ailment was sent for and came back the following day.
The Gernistorch beacon has been on the roll since before the present book was opened.

 1609.  Nobody has queried this since it was entered, and nobody is likely to: The

The rough book has the Trorrael creature under a heading the fair copy does not use. The

handrail at berth 102 was found loose at one end and was refastened. The Nuinagrist cargo
was written at the foot of the page and moved up when the page was recopied.


SECTION 16 -- Third round, against the ebb

The deputy of the reach records that low cloud and no wind at all made the ink run and that
the entries were gone over afterwards. The chain at berth 84 was ranged along the quay,
counted, and returned to its locker. Nothing came up the reach between the second glass of
the forenoon and dawn, which the night clerk entered with some relief. The Jaeskoameal cargo
was entered late and the entry was not queried. A slip of paper concerning the Thidridette
pennant was found in the chest and filed properly.

 1610.  A finding of the survey, carried across into the round record: The berth number of
        the Hymbegale watch is greater than the berth number of the Sishydric keeper.
        Entered in a steady hand and not gone over at any later date.
 1611.  Written into the margin first and moved here when the fair copy was made: The
        Krirenlull watch is berthed no further east than berth 10. The outer office copy
        carries the same wording letter for letter.

A rope was left coiled at berth 15 and nobody would own it. The night clerk holds that the
tide table is a glass out and has said so in each of the close of the year books. No pilot
was available before the change of the watch, and the round was held back accordingly. The
account for the Vrilleawake watch remains open pending a weight certificate. The Lialaensail
rig was read back to the keeper, who had nothing to add.

 1612.  The pilot had this from the quay and the quay had it from the round: The berth
        number of the Figrufever ailment is even. Struck once in error and written again
        identically beneath. The rough book has it identically, down to the wording.
 1613.  Noted at the change of the watch by both the outgoing and the incoming clerk: The
        Sethelle pennant lies somewhere to the east of the Frysseamsail rig. This was taken
        as settled from the hour it was written. This one the office has never had cause to
        query.

The inspector of holds finds the drainage along the whole quay worse than in the opening of
the year and says so plainly. A fog came up the reach with the flood and went out again with
the ebb. The clerk who keeps the rough book went over the entries for the Chiadeispan watch
and let them stand. Two pages of the previous book have come loose and want rebinding. The
spelling of the Skarleareth home port was corrected in the fair copy and left alone here.

 1614.  Neither queried nor amended since the day it was taken: None of the following lie in
        berths 71 through 76: the Gokriamor keeper, the Nankaedalgia ailment, the
        Plothitorch beacon, the Quillantithe toll band and the Glorkuirmark toll band. It
        was read out at the muster and nobody spoke against it. It stands in the same terms
        in the quarter's summary.
 1615.  The Kreguitariff toll band is not berthed at berth 104. No query was raised against
        this line at the muster or afterwards. The harbourmaster initialled the page and
        this line with it.

The pilot reported the channel shifted by something under the depth of a bucket and asked
for a sounding. The under-harbourmaster reports berth 83 sound in every particular. A hand
lamp was found burning at berth 66 in daylight and was put out. A rule was made that no
entry be written in pencil alone, and it lasted a fortnight. The clerk who keeps the rough
book measured the settlement at the head of the quay and makes it the height of the guard
rail since the last survey.

 1616.  Read at the gate, entered at the office, and not since disturbed: The Kroadarne
        pennant occupies an even-numbered berth. The entry stands as the round left it. It
        was written in good light and there is no doubt about the reading.
 1617.  From the round walked along the quay before the tide turned: The berth number of the
        Buidraette pennant is greater than the berth number of the Trinuindar keeper.
        Nothing in the later rounds contradicted it.
 1618.  Determined at the forenoon inspection and entered the same hour: Exactly 4 berths
        lie between the Jearrenlull watch and the Vrirdiolvang rig. It was confirmed on the
        round following and carried forward.

A lighter broke her moorings in the night and was recovered without damage to anything. The
Voudoblaze beacon was read out at the muster and answered for. The glass was read at the
turn of the glass and again at dusk, and the two readings agreed. The entry for the
Quegruigaff rig was the last made before the light failed. The warden of the outer moorings
has known the Makaflake cargo on the roll for longer than the present clerks.

 1619.  On the authority of the keeper of the book, who was present throughout: The
        Gaisenstay rig is berthed no further east than berth 23. Nothing further was added
        to this line in the whole of the quarter. The margin here is blank, which the office
        takes to mean no objection.
 1620.  Written out again after the first entry was spoiled: One and the same berth carries
        the Thiaskeish pennant and the Shuidriscar home port. That much is certain and is
        entered as certain. It needed no query and received none.
 1621.  The following was established beyond argument on the round: Exactly 9 berths lie
        between the Bloamiflame beacon and the Tasaenboom rig. The clerk who wrote it was
        asked and stands by it.
 1622.  Entered in ink at once, the matter being plain enough: The Wurmequota toll band
        occupies an odd-numbered berth. The clerk initialled it and the harbourmaster let it
        stand. The rough book agrees, and so does the copy held in the outer office.
 1623.  Confirmed against the previous quarter and found to stand: The Grireth home port and
        the Musmark toll band are recorded at the same berth. Checked at the next round and
        found to want no correction. Taken as settled from that day, and nothing since has
        unsettled it.

The wind stood in one quarter for six days together and then went right round in a night. A
receipt was issued for dues paid in cash and the counterfoil filed. Every entry in this
quarter's book was read back and agreed before the book was closed. A note against the

The quay was clear of stacked goods by the second bell after noon, which the standing orders

Frost lay on the coping until the striking of the hour and made the walking slow. There was
a squall that took one glass to pass over and a swell with it, though neither was enough to
stop the work. Nothing was landed on the north quay that morning; the cranes stood idle
until the first glass of the afternoon. A complete reading of the roll was made at the close
and no discrepancy was found. The key to the outer cupboard was lost and found again behind
the stove.

Snow lay on the quay for the better part of two days and was swept into the water. The clerk
of the health return entered a swell that never broke against the forenoon and nothing at
all against the afternoon. The assistant tallyman reports smoke from the tar sheds and adds
that the round was walked anyway. Rain in the night filled the gullies and they were still
running at the turn of the tide. There was a dry wind from the shoals and a swell with it,
though neither was enough to stop the work.

A survey of the wall behind berth 68 was ordered in the summer and is outstanding. A hand

        west to east. The outer office copy carries the same wording letter for letter. Two
        hands wrote this page and neither disputes this line.
 1789.  The finding of the second round, the first having been walked in poor light: The
        Keistuifever ailment lies within the last 27 berths of the reach. The rough book
        agrees, and so does the copy held in the outer office.
 1790.  A plain finding, and entered in the plain form: The Joundilboom rig is berthed
        somewhere east of the Seliolwyn keeper, though not necessarily beside it. It has
        stood in these words through two fair copies.

Payment was refused on one account and the matter passed to the outer office. The clerk who
entered the Stabriasyrn creature has since left the office. The kerb at berth 119 was reset
after it moved the depth of a bucket in the frost. Dues were collected at the quarter bell
and the receipts entered in the other book. The capstan at berth 38 turns stiffly and has
been greased.

 1791.  The following stands as entered and has not been questioned: The Kreguitariff toll
        band falls in the western stretch, berths 1 through 16. The clerk read it back and
        the keeper let it pass. It has been true in every book the office holds.
 1792.  Copied into the fair book the same evening and not altered since: There are exactly
        11 berths separating the Stoadellevy toll band from the Blaillamp beacon. The slate
        agreed before it was wiped, for what that is worth. The line was gone over in ink
        and is the clearer for it.
 1793.  Taken down in the rain and copied out dry: Walking the quay eastward, the inspector
        reaches the Thonnellarne pennant before the Plirmiadusk creature. The margin here is
        blank, which the office takes to mean no objection. The entry was made before the
        light went and needs no correction.
 1794.  On the authority of the keeper of the book, who was present throughout: The
        Tralliadmash cargo is berthed somewhere east of the Wigleam beacon, though not
        necessarily beside it. Entered in a steady hand and not gone over at any later date.
 1795.  Determined at the forenoon inspection and entered the same hour: The Sweliodvas
        keeper is berthed somewhere west of the Huibriodmash cargo, though not necessarily
        beside it. The clerk of the outer berths saw it and had nothing to add. The keeper
        signed beside it, which he does not always trouble to do.

Berth 97 was let and re-let twice in the same week, which the dues clerk queried. A hand
lamp was found burning at berth 44 in daylight and was put out. The hard standing at berth
31 is breaking up at the edges and wants attention. The water point at berth 24 ran slow and
the strainer was found blocked. The apron at berth 32 drains the wrong way and puddles after
cloud low enough to hide the far shore.

 1796.  Nobody has queried this since it was entered, and nobody is likely to: The Natiyrn
        creature and the Wurmequota toll band occupy adjacent berths. This one the office
        has never had cause to query. Taken as settled from that day, and nothing since has
        unsettled it.
 1797.  Written while the matter was fresh and not improved upon afterwards: Sailing east,
        the three are met in this order: the Stoadellevy toll band, then the Goassoatorch
        beacon, then the Lurkumund home port. That much is certain and is entered as
        certain.
 1798.  Settled between the clerks before the book was closed for the day: The Soarglass
        watch shares a berth with the Thinrate toll band. Both the rough book and the slate
        had it this way before the slate was wiped.
 1799.  The Treskilaemia ailment is berthed no further west than berth 97. The clerk who
        wrote it was asked and stands by it. Nothing further was added to this line in the
        whole of the quarter.
 1800.  Entered in the rough book that forenoon and copied here without change: The
        Blourchill ailment lies somewhere to the west of the Skerloanthan keeper. This line
        was copied twice and reads the same both times.

The keeper of the lamp store asks that dues be taken at the gate rather than on the quay.
The store room was counted through and the count agreed with the book within a little. Dues
were taken at the opening of the gates and the receipts entered against the quarter. The
store was locked and the key held by the assistant tallyman for the whole of the week. One
receipt was written out twice and the duplicate destroyed in front of a witness.

 1801.  Read at the gate, entered at the office, and not since disturbed: The Tanaemia
        ailment is berthed somewhere west of the Faendemark toll band, though not
        necessarily beside it. This line was not disputed by anybody with standing to
        dispute it.
 1802.  Attested by two hands at the change of the watch: Reading west to east, the
        Shuifuinmund home port comes before the Stoubrokrate toll band, and the Stoubrokrate
        toll band before the Kokrelague ailment. Both rounds of that day gave the same
        answer.
 1803.  Set down at the water point while the tally was going on: The harbourmaster counts
        exactly 1 of these within berths 64 through 80: the Kloamaenith creature, the
        Joarliurn creature, the Hokiostallow cargo, the Grodreiturn watch and the
        Fragolquota toll band. Struck once in error and written again identically beneath.
 1804.  The quarter's book has this in one hand throughout: Exactly 1 of the following lie
        in berths 65 through 74: the Pluirtoalloc keeper, the Kuitoax creature, the
        Thairlaimeal cargo, the Vriarirelle pennant, the Briarebb watch and the Snebrearturn
        watch. This was taken as settled from the hour it was written.
 1805.  A finding of the survey, carried across into the round record: Reading west to east,
        the Swemodresin cargo comes before the Troatystyrn creature, and the Troatystyrn
        creature before the Tigreanrate toll band. Entered last in the run and checked first
        on the round after. It was confirmed on the round following and carried forward.

The Jifiomor keeper was left out of the first draft of this page and added later. Berth 26
was measured again and found to agree with the plan. Rain in the night filled the gullies
and they were still running at the setting of the night watch. The store was locked and the
key held by the keeper of the book for the whole of the week. Dues were remitted in one case
on the harbourmaster's own authority.

 1806.  The keeper's own account, taken down and read back to him: The berth number of the
        Trurdeabark cargo is greater than the berth number of the Spesagrun keeper. The
        harbourmaster initialled the page and this line with it. The outer office was sent
        this and returned no query.
 1807.  Entered against the round of that forenoon: The Zivearate toll band occupies an
        odd-numbered berth. No query was raised against this line at the muster or
        afterwards. This was checked from the water as well as from the quay.
 1808.  The rough book has it in these words, and so does this: The Paiseallel creature lies
        within the last 12 berths of the reach. Countersigned at the quarter bell, the entry
        standing unamended. Copied into the fair book the same evening without alteration.
 1809.  From the rough book, in the words the clerk used at the time: The Kloadette pennant
        precedes the Slelaeroon pennant, which in turn precedes the Pronnolresin cargo,
        reading west to east. The line was numbered, initialled and left alone.
 1810.  Written up from the slate before it was wiped for the next round: The berth number
        of the Fraenbeam beacon is odd. The outer office copy carries the same wording
        letter for letter. The finding was not contested by anybody present.

The stone at berth 68 is worn hollow and will want replacing before long. The chain at berth
42 was ranged along the quay, counted, and returned to its locker. The quarter closed with
the rolls as they stood at its opening and no change entered against any of them. The
Driodialgia ailment gave no trouble whatever and is entered here only because the form
requires it. The spelling of the Weshospan watch was corrected in the fair copy and left
alone here.

 1811.  Entered from the pilot's own account of the reach: Exactly 1 of the following lie in
        berths 22 through 51: the Vrigrun keeper, the Lournainarne pennant, the Braeforglass
        watch, the Jaekreaspark beacon and the Nymiolband toll band. The line was gone over
        in ink after the pencil faded, and not otherwise changed. It has stood in these
        words through two fair copies.
 1812.  The Birlelmash cargo falls in the eastern stretch, berths 93 through 120. The clerk
        of the outer berths saw it and had nothing to add.

Weather for the week: rain heavy enough to stop the tally on four days and nothing
remarkable on the others. The Spipovang rig was not inspected this quarter, the last
inspection being recent enough. A loose plank at berth 7 was nailed down and the nail heads
punched below the surface. The office was shut for half a day while the floor was relaid.
The first entry for the Fryklevy toll band in this book was struck and written again below.

 1813.  Entered after the round was walked a second time on the same day: The Puissaelevy
        toll band and the Wigleam beacon are recorded at the same berth. The quarter closed
        with this line exactly as it opened. That much is certain and is entered as certain.
 1814.  Entered in ink at once, the matter being plain enough: The Thagreclew rig lies
        somewhere to the east of the Gezamkell keeper. The line was gone over in ink and is
        the clearer for it. Nothing was added to it and nothing taken away.
 1815.  Taken at the gate and carried straight to the book: The Snikruimeal cargo occupies
        an even-numbered berth. The keeper signed beside it, which he does not always
        trouble to do.
 1816.  One of the findings the outer office asked to have set out plainly: The Snedrionidge
        pennant lies within the last 29 berths of the reach. It stands in the same terms in
        the quarter's summary. The rough book agrees, and so does the copy held in the outer
        office.

The Skonnomund home port has been written three ways in three books and one way in this one.
The heading under which the Zirteadue toll band stands was altered in the opening of the
year and altered back. The Beafysturn creature is one of the entries the copyist marked for
attention and then let alone. The clerk asked whether the Quachill ailment should be entered
at all and was told that it should. The Kirraemeal cargo was not inspected this quarter, the
last inspection being recent enough.

 1817.  The pilot had this from the quay and the quay had it from the round: Walking the
        quay eastward, the inspector reaches the Zesteirbark cargo before the Bradralt home
        port.
 1818.  The berth number of the Quigrioboom rig is greater than the berth number of the
        Ploudvas keeper. This line was not disputed by anybody with standing to dispute it.

The morning clerk reports the stores in good order and the dues fully collected. Silt was
carted from the head of the basin and tipped where the orders require. A second copy of the
roll was made and is kept in the outer office against a fire. The apron at berth 78 drains
the wrong way and puddles after a squall that took one glass to pass over. Fuel for the
office stove was drawn against the quarter and entered elsewhere.

 1819.  Written out again after the first entry was spoiled: Between the Siaskodbell watch
        and the Jaengaithith creature the ledger counts exactly 4 berths. The clerk who
        wrote it was asked and stands by it.
 1820.  The under-harbourmaster is satisfied, having walked the ground himself: The
        Suirkasail rig lies immediately to the east of the Slidrolweed cargo. Struck once in
        error and written again identically beneath. Two hands wrote this page and neither
        disputes this line.

A dispute about the rate of dues was settled by reference to the standing orders. The
Slaneirnyard rig is written in ink over a pencil line that has not been rubbed out. The
rounds were walked on every day the orders require and on four days besides. Berth 62 is the
only one on its stretch with a working standpipe. The lamp standard at berth 105 was relit
at the evening tally.

 1821.  The finding of the second round, the first having been walked in poor light: The
        Pluzaellull watch is berthed somewhere east of the Blastesard creature, though not
        necessarily beside it. This one the office has never had cause to query.
 1822.  Held back one day for confirmation and then entered as it stood: The harbourmaster
        counts exactly 2 of these within berths 32 through 53: the Tortosorne home port, the
        Bruimvask home port, the Pateimgale watch, the Giokolgaff rig, the Jaepurgleam
        beacon and the Jygoaquota toll band. Confirmed at the evening tally and carried
        forward unchanged.

The wind backed twice before the reading of the standing orders and settled very near where
it had begun. A warm wind in the autumn took the frost off the quay in a single forenoon.
The forenoon was fine and the afternoon was not, and the round fell in the better half. The
tide was slack and the wind against it, which is the condition that makes the narrows
awkward. The keeper of the book asks that the weather be entered before the tide and not
after, as the form requires.

 1823.  Confirmed by two clerks working independently of one another: The Blealorne home
        port shares a berth with the Shirmothrate toll band. The clerk initialled it and the
        harbourmaster let it stand.

One receipt was written out twice and the duplicate destroyed in front of a witness. The
entry for the Hokiostallow cargo was the last made before the light failed. The keeper of
the lamp store found the gate at berth 58 unlocked and locked it himself. The Fizospan watch
was read out at the muster and answered for. The Tarledkell keeper was named in a complaint
that was afterwards withdrawn.


SECTION 18 -- The pilot's account of the reach

A fog came up the reach with the flood and went out again with the ebb. Weather held fair
for the whole of the round and the entries were made in comfort. The copyist entered the
weather twice and the tide not at all, which has been corrected in the fair copy. The glass
moved not at all for three days, which the clerk on loan from the outer office says is the
worst sign of the lot. The officer who walks the eastern end entered a dry wind from the
shoals against the forenoon and nothing at all against the afternoon.

 1824.  Entered under the standing orders and needing no further authority: Sailing east,
        the three are met in this order: the Huibriodmash cargo, then the Peibylmast rig,
        then the Sethelle pennant.
 1825.  Noted at the change of the watch by both the outgoing and the incoming clerk: There
        are exactly 1 berth separating the Kleidruklamp beacon from the Trerronmor keeper.
        The slate agreed before it was wiped, for what that is worth. It was read out at the
        muster and nobody spoke against it.
 1826.  The Pluisearmeal cargo lies immediately to the east of the Tuiloneen pennant. The
        keeper was shown the entry and made no remark.
 1827.  Taken down in the rain and copied out dry: The Nankaedalgia ailment lies somewhere
        to the west of the Jaepurgleam beacon. It needed no query and received none.

Berth 91 and the two beside it were inspected in one pass to save walking. The chain at
berth 27 was shortened by two links at the keeper's request. The cash box was counted at the
last bell before dark and agreed with the day's entries. Rubbish accumulated at berth 103
and was carted away before the second bell after noon. Berth 8 and the one beside it share a
single water point, which is a nuisance.

 1828.  The Thastern home port occupies an even-numbered berth. This was among the lines
        read aloud when the book was closed. It was the plainest finding of the round.
 1829.  Neither queried nor amended since the day it was taken: The Prokeen pennant precedes
        the Skotrikurn creature, which in turn precedes the Roruistrate toll band, reading
        west to east. Entered in a steady hand and not gone over at any later date. The
        entry stands as the round left it.
 1830.  The officer of the reach saw it himself and required no corroboration: Exactly 2
        berths lie between the Giangevigil watch and the Skorriordue toll band. The matter
        was plain and the entry is plain with it.
 1831.  Carried into this book from the survey papers without alteration: The Sturniclew rig
        precedes the Biriorchill ailment, which in turn precedes the Kraitryrwick beacon,
        reading west to east. The entry was made before the light went and needs no
        correction. Countersigned at the quarter bell, the entry standing unamended.
 1832.  Taken as good on the authority of the clerk who walked the stretch: None of the
        following lie in berths 9 through 22: the Goussykresin cargo, the Toastoadrot
        ailment, the Giveiclew rig, the Mengydmast rig, the Spoudriastay rig and the
        Vrybouflare beacon.

The paperwork for the Krioresin cargo was found complete and wants nothing further. A
visiting clerk from upriver spent two days in the office and took away three copies. The
morning clerk walked berth 19 twice, the second time in better light. The bar shoaled
through the spring and has since scoured out again on its own. A note against the
Snilairblaze beacon in the margin has been rubbed away.

 1833.  Copied into the fair book the same evening and not altered since: The berth number
        of the Klorkothosis ailment is even. The finding was not contested by anybody
        present. Both the rough book and the slate had it this way before the slate was
        wiped.
 1834.  Checked against the previous quarter before it was written: The berth 60 entry rules
        out the Skaermeakard creature. Nothing was added to it and nothing taken away.

The quarter's lamp oil ran to rather more than was allowed for, owing to fog standing in the
roads. The wind backed twice before the first bell and settled very near where it had begun.
A list of the office's books was made and is kept inside the lid of the chest. The officer
of stores asks that the outer office send the forms earlier in the autumn. The Zesteirbark
cargo was inspected in passing and no note was thought necessary.

 1835.  This was the finding of the round and is entered as such: Between the Traishesidge
        pennant and the Gloangemeen pennant the ledger counts exactly 9 berths. The keeper
        signed beside it, which he does not always trouble to do.
 1836.  Established at the forenoon inspection and confirmed at the evening tally: Exactly 1
        berth lie between the Snermuikgale watch and the Spaetide watch. It stands in the
        same terms in the quarter's summary.

The rough books for the quarter are bound separately and held in the outer office. The
quarter's soundings were taken, entered, and compared with those of the opening of the year.
The health return for the quarter was completed and filed with the quarter's papers. A
complete reading of the roll was made at the close and no discrepancy was found. One page of
the quarter's book was spoiled and recopied, and both copies are held.

 1837.  Recorded by the officer of the reach, who had it from the keeper: None of the
        following lie in berths 58 through 72: the Wengoasith creature, the Juglass watch,
        the Sturniclew rig and the Treilamp beacon. Nobody has found cause to go behind this
        entry. The quarter closed with this line exactly as it opened.
 1838.  The harbourmaster asked for this in writing and here it is: The berth number of the
        Paiseallel creature is greater than the berth number of the Zeithodreth home port.
        No hand has been laid on this line since it was written.
 1839.  The berth number of the Traishesidge pennant is greater than the berth number of the
        Vaichewyn keeper. The line was gone over in ink and is the clearer for it. The
        harbourmaster initialled the page and this line with it.

The weather in the spring was as it usually is, and the book records nothing further about
it. Drainage at berth 106 backed up during the rain and was cleared by hand. The clerk of
the outer berths asked that berth 23 be looked at again before the close of the close of the
year. The roll was read through at the close of the quarter and every entry on it accounted
for. The sky cleared at the turn of the glass and stayed clear until the following forenoon.

 1840.  From the day's findings, in the order they were taken: The Briarebb watch and the
        Kravang rig are recorded at the same berth. Checked at the next round and found to
        want no correction.
 1841.  Carried over from the page before, where the ink had run: The Treigearlevy toll band
        is berthed no further west than berth 95. Taken as settled from that day, and
        nothing since has unsettled it. The clerk initialled it and the harbourmaster let it
        stand.
 1842.  Read back at the muster and agreed by both clerks present: The Blourchill ailment
        falls in the western stretch, berths 1 through 10. Entered last in the run and
        checked first on the round after. This was checked from the water as well as from
        the quay.
 1843.  Written into the margin first and moved here when the fair copy was made: Walking
        the quay eastward, the inspector reaches the Winkekbeam beacon before the Droglim
        beacon. Nothing in the later rounds contradicted it. This line was copied twice and
        reads the same both times.
 1844.  The Braeforglass watch shares a berth with the Falluirnyrn creature. No amendment
        has been entered against it since. Both rounds of that day gave the same answer.

A new rule about the ordering of entries was posted and is already ignored. The keeper of
the lamp store and the officer who walks the eastern end divided the rounds between them for
the week. The office lamp was refilled twice in the week, which is more than usual. The
officer who walks the eastern end has asked twice for the numbering of the entries to be
started afresh each quarter. The office took delivery of oakum and entered it against the
quarter.

 1845.  From the rough book, in the words the clerk used at the time: Berth 113 does not
        hold the Seliolwyn keeper. It was written in good light and there is no doubt about
        the reading. The ink is clear here and the reading is not in doubt.
 1846.  Taken on the second round, when the first had been doubted: Reading west to east,
        the Tuander pennant comes before the Driodholm home port, and the Driodholm home
        port before the Ziorkasvask home port.
 1847.  A finding of the survey, carried across into the round record: The harbourmaster
        counts exactly 2 of these within berths 60 through 75: the Dunnadmor keeper, the
        Sheisoaric keeper, the Labamish pennant and the Mengydmast rig. Struck once in error
        and written again identically beneath. It was read out at the muster and nobody
        spoke against it.
 1848.  Written while the matter was fresh and not improved upon afterwards: The berth
        number of the Jearrombeam beacon is even. The line was gone over in ink after the

 1849.  Walking the quay eastward, the inspector reaches the Plaevouselle pennant before the
        Kryzadidge pennant. It has stood in these words through two fair copies.

The quarter ended with the whole reach in service and no berth out of use. The paint on the
numbering plate at berth 46 has gone and wants renewing. A survey of the decking at berth 84
was ordered and is not yet begun. Berth 32 appears in the rough book for a day on which the
round was not walked. The inspector of holds counted the office's stock of chalk and slate
and found it short.

 1850.  One of the quarter's plain findings, entered here in order: The Shaikrealalt home
        port is berthed immediately west of the Busbark cargo, with nothing between them.
 1851.  The office copy and the rough book agree in this: The Paebraikish pennant lies
        within the last 3 berths of the reach. It needed no query and received none. It was
        confirmed on the round following and carried forward.

The office stove smoked through the season of gales and the chimney was swept at last.
Nothing has been entered against the Buidraette pennant since the book was opened. The
Shiatrodmor keeper is entered here because the standing orders require it and for no other
reason. A quantity of rubbish had blown into berth 65 and was cleared at the quarter bell.
The clerk asked whether the Laitrelthan keeper should be entered at all and was told that it
should.

 1852.  Given to the clerk by the quay warden directly and taken as good: The Hoangarorne
        home port falls in the eastern stretch, berths 102 through 120. Confirmed at the

 1853.  Checked on the ground and checked again in the book: None of the following lie in
        berths 77 through 103: the Sasoalmeal cargo, the Kryzadidge pennant, the Triosis
        ailment, the Snudurglass watch and the Jaisimark toll band. The entry was made
