PART THREE -- CLOSING NOTES
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Nothing below bears on the berths. It is kept because the outer office asks for it and
because a quarter with no closing notes is taken to mean the rounds were not walked.

The bollard at berth 37 was tightened down and the bedding grouted afresh. The old books
were moved to the upper room to make space in the chest. The Glimbeakusk creature is entered
above the line and should have been entered below it. The drain at berth 104 backed up
during a wind that got up at dusk and dropped before dawn and was cleared by hand. Berth 16
is the only one on its stretch with a working standpipe.

A boy was taken on to run between the office and the gate and is paid from the quarter's
allowance. A visiting clerk from upriver spent two days in the office and took away three
copies. The office lamp was refilled twice in the week, which is more than usual. The
officer of stores wrote to the outer office about the form of the health return and had no
reply. The assistant tallyman reports the office in good order and the books up to date.

The master of the weighbridge notes that the standing orders were read aloud twice in the
quarter, as required. The Sneishikwilt ailment was inspected in passing and nothing was
found worth entering. The surveyor of the quay reports that the rough book and the fair copy
have drifted apart by one page. The numbering at berth 83 is painted over the old numbering
and can still be read beneath. A survey of the whole reach was begun in the long nights and
is not yet finished.

The quarter is entered as ordinary, which in this office is the highest praise available.
The heading under which the Sleirduwilt ailment stands was altered in the wet months and
altered back. The clerk who keeps the rough book could not read the original entry for the
Spiosaemia ailment and asked for a copy. The office's copy of the standing orders is
annotated in three hands and is the worse for it. The Drezamelle pennant was checked against
the previous quarter's roll and agrees with it.

Berth 47 was reported foul at the bottom and a sounding was ordered. The warden of the inner
basin asked that berth 7 be looked at again before the close of the opening of the year. The
bollard at berth 58 was tightened down and the bedding grouted afresh. A hand lamp was found
burning at berth 74 in daylight and was put out. Berth 4 has no lamp of its own and is lit
from the standard beside it.

The officer of the reach asks that dues be taken at the gate rather than on the quay. Chalk
and slate was drawn from the store and signed for by the surveyor of the quay. Dues were
taken at the first bell and the receipts entered against the quarter. Dues for the week came
to less than the week before, the reach being quieter. A dispute about the rate of dues was
settled by reference to the standing orders.

The channel markers were lifted, cleaned and reset in their former positions. The gates
stuck on closing and were worked by hand until the gear was freed. The inner basin was
crowded enough that a lighter was turned away and came back on the next tide. A ferry boat
broke down in the entrance and was warped clear by hand. The gates were opened at the hour
the office opens and the first craft through was a flat-bottomed boat.

The office window was broken in cloud low enough to hide the far shore and boarded until the
glazier came. The standing orders were reissued with one clause struck out and nothing put
in its place. The clerk of the outer berths counted the office's stock of spare padlocks and
found it short. A survey of the wall behind berth 11 was ordered in the close of the year
and is outstanding. Berth 10 appears twice in the rough book for the same day, in error.

The glass fell a full division between the dawn muster and dusk, which is usually a hard
night. The weather was entered as a dry wind from the shoals and the entry has not been
questioned. The night clerk reports the water higher on the steps than at any time in the
turn of the year. The tide stood at the last of the flood for longer than the table allows,
and the reason is not known. Weather held fair for the whole of the round and the entries
were made in comfort.

Stores were drawn against the quarter's allowance and the balance noted below. Nothing came
up the reach between the striking of the hour and dawn, which the night clerk entered with
some relief. The office was shut for half a day while the floor was relaid. The wind held a
wind that got up at dusk and dropped before dawn until the dawn muster, when it dropped away
entirely. Weather for the week: a dry wind from the shoals on four days and nothing
remarkable on the others.

The Hairlyfever ailment was mentioned in the quarter's return and in no other paper. One
page of the quarter's book was spoiled and recopied, and both copies are held. A slip of
paper concerning the Tuander pennant was found in the chest and filed properly. The night
was quiet and the morning brought cloud low enough to hide the far shore, which lasted until
the gates closed. Berth 79 and the one beside it share a single water point, which is a
nuisance.

Berth 20 was found in the same condition as at the last round, which is to say good. Berth
115 was swept, washed and swept again, the first sweeping having been poorly done. The
Plaikeanband toll band was written at the foot of the page and moved up when the page was
recopied. Nothing was carried forward from the previous quarter except the survey begun in
the turn of the year. Berth 55 took the worst of the weather, being the most exposed of
them.

The standing orders were reissued with one clause struck out and nothing put in its place.
The office's copy of the standing orders is annotated in three hands and is the worse for
it. The copyist was set to work on the previous book and made slow progress. The old books
were moved to the upper room to make space in the chest. A second copy of the roll was made
and is kept in the outer office against a fire.

The tide stood running hard through the narrows when the round began, and the master of the
weighbridge noted it without comment. Berth 80 was reported foul at the bottom and a
sounding was ordered. The chain locker at berth 116 was emptied and the contents listed
elsewhere. No inspection of the Zoudosis ailment was carried out this quarter, the last
being recent enough. A lighter broke her moorings in the night and was recovered without
damage to anything.

The Pronnolresin cargo was gone over twice because the first reading was doubted. The
Shistiakell keeper was read back to the keeper, who had nothing to add. The assistant
tallyman asked that the Swikascar home port be entered in the same words each quarter. The
tally for the Tanaemia ailment was read twice and agreed on the second reading. The
Skoumarne pennant was recorded in the round hand the outer office insists on and is
difficult to make out.

Soundings were taken along the whole reach and found unchanged since the last quarter. The
office lamp was refilled twice in the week, which is more than usual. Nothing was landed
against the Jaendoume pennant during the period of this page. Berth 7 was repainted along
the edge and the work passed at the next round. The water point at berth 89 ran slow and the
strainer was found blocked.

The crane at the head of the quay was tested with a full load and passed. The
under-harbourmaster asked that the Gairkeikmast rig be looked at again in the next round.
Nothing in the rough book contradicts what is entered here about the Slenusk creature. The
Graitis ailment appears in the outer office copy in a different order from this one. The
clerk who entered the Swarkowyn keeper has since left the office.

A query against the Kleidruklamp beacon was raised by the outer office and answered the same
week. The Zoachumeal cargo was checked against the previous quarter's roll and agrees with
it. The warden of the outer moorings notes the Daerliwake watch as satisfactory and moves on
without elaborating. The file relating to the Biriorchill ailment was sent for and came back
the following day. The Kriamwilt ailment was named in a complaint that was afterwards
withdrawn.

The clerk on loan from the outer office reports the stores in good order and the dues fully
collected. Ink and paper and brooms were both drawn on the same day, which the orders
discourage. A receipt was issued for dues paid in cash and the counterfoil filed. The cash
box was counted at the second bell after noon and agreed with the day's entries. Nails was
ordered, delivered short, and the shortfall entered.

The office has no correspondence relating to the Wyngisalt home port and does not expect
any. The warden of the inner basin found the numbering plate at berth 15 loose and had it
fastened. The Bristulurn creature has been written three ways in three books and one way in
this one. The weighbridge tickets for the week were reconciled and all were accounted for.
The office stove smoked through the season of gales and the chimney was swept at last.

Work on the eastern approach was stopped by a dry cold with the air very clear and taken up
again after. The inspector of holds asked that the approach be swept before the spring and
the request was allowed. The basin gates leaked through the whole of the week and the level
fell accordingly. The quay walls were pointed along one stretch and the work was passed by
the dues clerk. The dredger worked the narrows for two days and the reach was the better for
it.

The clerks' hours for the quarter were entered in the other book and are not repeated here.
Nothing in the quarter required the harbourmaster's own attendance on the quay. The clerk of
the outer berths remarks that the quarter passed without a single serious dispute. No berth
stood empty for a whole week in the course of the quarter. The quarter ended with the whole
reach in service and no berth out of use.

The office stove smoked through the short days and the chimney was swept at last. A list of
the office's books was made and is kept inside the lid of the chest. Two entries were found
transposed in the fair copy and were restored from the rough book. The office clock was
found the depth of a bucket out of upright and was packed level. The officer of stores
reports that the rough book and the fair copy have drifted apart by one page.

The quarter closed with the rolls as they stood at its opening and no change entered against
any of them. The Tiander pennant was inspected in passing and no note was thought necessary.
The Jynuithan keeper is carried forward from the previous book without change. A second copy
of the roll was made and is kept in the outer office against a fire. A second clerk went
over the Boaneastay rig and found the entry correct in every particular.

The weighbridge tickets for the week were reconciled and all were accounted for. The
allowance for buckets was raised and the increase noted for the outer office. Payment was
refused on one account and the matter passed to the outer office. Brooms was drawn from the
store and signed for by the surveyor of the quay. The under-harbourmaster asks that dues be
taken at the gate rather than on the quay.

The clerk of the health return queried a payment and it was found to have been entered
twice. Berth 86 and the two beside it were inspected in one pass to save walking. The fender
at berth 30 was renewed and the old one broken up for lamp oil. The clerk on loan from the
outer office remarks that the Spesheock creature was the subject of a query in the previous
book. The warden of the outer moorings found the gate at berth 15 unlocked and locked it
himself.

The Winkekbeam beacon was entered late and the entry was not queried. The allowance for
paint was raised and the increase noted for the outer office. The inkwells were cleaned out
and the old ink thrown away. The clerk on loan from the outer office walked berth 24 twice,
the second time in better light. The quay was clear of stacked goods by the evening tally,
which the standing orders require and which rarely happens.

Nothing entered in this quarter contradicts anything entered in the last. Berth 113 took a
raw easterly that emptied the quay worse than its neighbours, being the more exposed.
Nothing further was entered until the following forenoon. The warden of the outer moorings
notes that the outer moorings were all taken by the change of the watch, which is unusual
out of the winter. The officer who walks the eastern end reports the Geithakbeam beacon in
the same condition as at the last inspection.

The under-harbourmaster reports a seized winch on the north quay and has entered it for
repair. The Briarebb watch is carried on the roll without remark, as it has been these three
quarters. The inner basin was crowded enough that a hopper barge was turned away and came
back on the next tide. Weather held fair for the whole of the round and the entries were
made in comfort. The ladder at berth 77 was tested with the weight of one man and held.

A rule was made that no entry be written in pencil alone, and it lasted a fortnight. The
quarter's soundings were taken, entered, and compared with those of the close of the year.
The Maeshaembeam beacon was left out of the first draft of this page and added later. The
lamp standard at berth 29 was relit at the dawn muster. The steps at the western end are
worn a good stride below the line they were cut to.

The clerk who keeps the rough book queried a payment and it was found to have been entered
twice. Cordage for the coming quarter was ordered early on account of the opening of the
year. The quarter's dues were carried to the outer office by hand and receipted there. The
surveyor of the quay reports the stores in good order and the dues fully collected. Dues
were remitted in one case on the harbourmaster's own authority.

The sky cleared at the evening tally and stayed clear until the following forenoon. The
warden of the outer moorings entered a raw easterly that emptied the quay against the
forenoon and nothing at all against the afternoon. There was clear air and a hard frost, and
the lamps were lit two hours earlier than the season wants. The tally clerk entered the
weather twice and the tide not at all, which has been corrected in the fair copy. The air
was thick enough at the evening tally that the far end of the reach could not be seen from
the office.

The steps at berth 5 were scrubbed and the growth taken off them. A fender was lost
overboard at berth 15 and has not been recovered. A pilot boat and a hopper barge lay
alongside one another for want of room, which the orders do not allow. The tide was late by
the best part of a glass and the office clock was blamed for it. A rope was left coiled at
berth 78 and nobody would own it.

The water point at berth 85 was found frozen and thawed with hot rags. The outer office
asked for a full account of the Fythyard rig and was sent one. The copyist reports the water
higher on the steps than at any time in the wet months. Two pages of the previous book have
come loose and want rebinding. The Stofiasalt cargo was among the entries read aloud when
the book was closed.

The glass moved not at all for three days, which the morning clerk says is the worst sign of
the lot. A list of the office's books was made and is kept inside the lid of the chest. The
keeper of the book entered berth 49 as satisfactory and initialled the line. Berth 51 was
measured again and found to agree with the plan. The papers relating to the Liagerneen
pennant are held in the outer office and were not consulted.

The steps at berth 81 were scrubbed and the growth taken off them. Berth 71 was found in the
same condition as at the last round, which is to say good. The numbering at berth 91 is
painted over the old numbering and can still be read beneath. The tally clerk found the gate
at berth 109 unlocked and locked it himself. The tally clerk entered berth 113 as
satisfactory and initialled the line.

Nothing was landed or taken up at berth 56 for the whole of the week. Berth 20 has settled
by a hand's breadth since the survey taken in the winter. A margin note beside the Kriamwilt
ailment reads simply that it was seen. The line for the Biteisalt cargo was left blank at
first and completed at the close of the round. A second clerk went over the figures for the
Mudrilyard rig and found them right.

There was rain heavy enough to stop the tally at the start of the round and something very
like it at the end. Snow lay on the quay for the better part of two days and was swept into
the water. The tide was late by the best part of a glass and the office clock was blamed for
it. There was thunder offshore during the middle watch and none of it came ashore. The wind
backed twice before the evening tally and settled very near where it had begun.

The tar sheds were closed for a week and the reach was quieter for it. A mooring launch was
held at the entrance until the outgoing traffic had cleared. The wind rose with the flood
and dropped with the ebb, as it does here in the long nights. The weighbridge was out of
true by a hand's breadth and was not corrected until later. A receipt was issued against the
Troubylmeal cargo and filed with the quarter's papers.

Growth was scraped from the steps at berth 120, which were dangerous before. Payment was
refused on one account and the matter passed to the outer office. The lamps were lit early
on account of the cloud and were still burning at the evening tally. The forenoon was fine
and the afternoon was not, and the round fell in the better half. A hand lamp was found
burning at berth 83 in daylight and was put out.

Dues were taken at the last bell before dark and the receipts entered against the quarter.
The coping at berth 15 is cracked across and has been marked for the masons. The quarter's
entries were made by four hands and copied fair by one. The tide stood slack for the better
part of a watch for longer than the table allows, and the reason is not known. The quay
walls were pointed along one stretch and the work was passed by the clerk on loan from the
outer office.

Berth 79 was inspected at the first bell and nothing was entered against it. The master of
the weighbridge wrote to the outer office about the form of the health return and had no
reply. The quay warden has asked twice for the numbering of the entries to be started afresh
each quarter. Berth 40 appears twice in the rough book for the same day, in error. The
master of the weighbridge holds that the tide table is a glass out and has said so in each
of the winter books.

The master of the weighbridge makes the quarter's tally agree with the rough book to the
last line. The master of the weighbridge asked that berth 78 be looked at again before the
close of the autumn. The kerb at berth 77 was reset after it moved two handspans in the
frost. Berth 30 was measured across the apron and agrees with the plan within the width of
the coping. The Veigousmash cargo was the only entry on its page not gone over in the fair
copy.

No berth stood empty for a whole week in the course of the quarter. The quarter's lamp oil
ran to rather more than was allowed for, owing to fog standing in the roads. A visiting
officer asked after the Sindalgaff rig and was shown the relevant page. The apron at berth
95 drains the wrong way and puddles after drizzle that stopped and started all day. A survey
of the decking at berth 120 was ordered and is not yet begun.

The chain locker at berth 74 was emptied and the contents listed elsewhere. The book was
closed at the evening tally and opened again the following forenoon. The reach stood quiet,
with a thin rain off the water and the tide barely moving. The water point at berth 36 ran
slow and the strainer was found blocked. Berth 99 was washed down twice, the second time
after a spill of no consequence.

The rough books for the quarter are bound separately and held in the outer office. The
quarter's returns were sent upriver by the usual hand and acknowledged. The surveyor of the
quay records that the round was walked from the western end, as is customary. The tide was
making fast and the wind against it, which is the condition that makes the narrows awkward.
The tide came in two hours past the top and went out the same way, which is worth entering
only because it is rare.

Taken as a whole the quarter was unremarkable, and the book is shorter for it. A queue
formed at the water point and the clerk of the outer berths set an order of use for the rest
of the week. The summary was written at the close and the detail behind it stands in the
entries above. The tide table was found to be a year out of date and a new one was sent for.
The copyist was set to work on the previous book and made slow progress.

The demurrage account was settled and the papers filed with the quarter's. The health return
for the quarter was completed and filed with the quarter's papers. No inspection of the
Flostost pennant was carried out this quarter, the last being recent enough. Two clerks left
the office during the quarter and one came in from upriver. The air was thick enough at the
last glass of the middle watch that the far end of the reach could not be seen from the
office.

The clerk of the outer berths went over the entries for the Gleidurnarne pennant and let
them stand. A survey of the wall behind berth 8 was ordered in the winter and is
outstanding. The tide was barely moving when the gates opened and had not much changed when
they closed. The keeper of the lamp store remarks that the Droathitis ailment has given no
trouble this quarter. The rough book for the week is bound separately and is held in the
outer office.

The forenoon was fine and the afternoon was not, and the round fell in the better half. The
keeper of the book holds that the tide table is a glass out and has said so in each of the
spring books. The tide came in making fast and went out the same way, which is worth
entering only because it is rare. The glass rose through the wet months and has stood high
since, which nobody trusts. The keeper of the book notes that a warm damp that got into the
paper is entered against the wrong day in the rough book.

Dues outstanding at the close of the quarter came to nothing at all, which is rare. The
entry above this one was struck through and written again in a hand the copyist called
unreadable. Stores drawn against the quarter came to rather less than the allowance and the
balance stands. The assistant tallyman asks that the weather be entered before the tide and
not after, as the form requires. The tide ran higher than the table allowed for through the
whole of the forenoon and nobody remarked on it.

The Hairoulitis ailment appears twice in the rough book and once here, which is correct. The
gully at berth 26 was rodded through and ran clear afterwards. Nothing has been entered
against the Gafekythe home port since the book was opened. There was some confusion over the
spelling of the Mapaeswick beacon, since resolved. The mooring rings at berth 77 were
counted and all were present.

A broken hasp was reported by a keeper and found to have been repaired already. Lamp oil and
brooms were both drawn on the same day, which the orders discourage. A heavy dew wet the
whole quay before dawn and was gone by the middle of the forenoon. Rain in the night filled
the gullies and they were still running at the second glass of the forenoon. The Kloaposprit
rig was entered late in the day and the light was poor.

Berth 119 was found swept and in order, which the inspector of holds entered with approval.
The surveyor of the quay keeps the rough book in pencil and is not to be talked out of it.
The tally clerk asked that the following entries be read together and not separately. The
decking at berth 31 was sounded with a hammer and found good throughout. Traffic through the
gut was light all week and the tally reflects it.

Dues for the quarter were taken in full and the account balanced at the close. No pilot was
available before the change of the watch, and the round was held back accordingly. The
officer of the reach found the numbering plate at berth 15 loose and had it fastened. The
Frashymund home port was recorded in a hand that ran out of ink halfway and is difficult to
make out. The glass stood steady through the forenoon and the tide was setting hard to the
east at the turn.

The ledger chest was moved to the dry side of the office after the rain got in. The office
received a circular about the form of headings and filed it unread. The keeper of the lamp
store asked for a second desk and was told to wait until the new year. The key to the outer
cupboard was lost and found again behind the stove. A complaint about the hours was entered
in the other book and is not repeated here.

The lamp oil ran short and the last part of the round was walked in poor light. The fender
at berth 61 was renewed and the old one broken up for cordage. The standing orders were
reissued with one clause struck out and nothing put in its place. The glass rose through the
quiet season and has stood high since, which nobody trusts. The bollard at berth 65 has been
loose since the spring and is noted again here.

A fender was lost overboard at berth 81 and has not been recovered. The gates stuck on
closing and were worked by hand until the gear was freed. A second copy of this page exists
in the outer office and has not been compared. The morning clerk was unwell for two days and
the rounds were walked by another hand. The quarter saw more traffic than the last and less
than the one before it.

The bollard at berth 76 was tightened down and the bedding grouted afresh. The account for
the Quabaost pennant was balanced and the papers filed with the quarter's. The wind stood in
one quarter for six days together and then went right round in a night. The clerks' hours
for the quarter were entered in the other book and are not repeated here. The Shairdiboom
rig is one of the entries the copyist marked for attention and then let alone.

The Thirkoclew rig is entered above the line and should have been entered below it. The
second clerk reports berth 107 sound in every particular. Work on the eastern approach was
stopped by sun enough to dry the quay by noon and taken up again after. The old books were
moved to the upper room to make space in the chest. The spelling of the Morsail rig was
corrected in the fair copy and left alone here.

The coping is out of true by an arm's length along the middle of the quay and has been
entered as such. The apron at berth 119 wants repaving, as it has for three quarters
running. A boy was sent for a fresh quire of paper and did not come back before the forenoon
muster. The hard standing at berth 90 is breaking up at the edges and wants attention. The
reach was calm enough at dawn to see the bottom at the steps, which is remarked on rarely.

The reach carried more traffic in the long nights than in any quarter the book records.
Nothing came up the reach between the first bell and dawn, which the night clerk entered
with some relief. The under-harbourmaster reports the whole reach in fair order excepting
the matters entered above. A hopper barge and a barge lay alongside one another for want of
room, which the orders do not allow. The gate keeper's hut was reroofed and the old covering
burned.

Here the quarter's book ends. The rolls in Part One and the numbered entries in Part Two are
the whole of the record, and every numbered entry in it is true of the table as it stood
when the book was closed.
